aero-w1-q1.question: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all weather (clouds, rain) occur, with temperature falling as height increases?
aero-w1-q1.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest layer (up to about 11 km). Almost all water vapour and weather is here, and temperature falls with height. Trap: temperature also falls in the mesosphere, but there is no weather there; the stratosphere holds the ozone layer and its temperature rises.

aero-w1-q2.question: In the ISA model, what is the temperature at 4 km altitude? (sea level 288.15 K, lapse rate 6.5 K/km)
aero-w1-q2.explanation: T = 288.15 − 6.5 × 4 = 288.15 − 26 = 262.15 K. Temperature falls as you climb in the troposphere. Trap: 314.15 K comes from adding the 26 K instead of subtracting it; 248.15 K from using a lapse rate of 10 K/km.

aero-w1-q3.question: At some altitude the pressure is 61,640 Pa and the temperature is 262.15 K. Taking R = 287 J/(kg·K) for air, what is the density?
aero-w1-q3.explanation: ρ = p/(RT) = 61,640 / (287 × 262.15) ≈ 0.819 kg/m³. Trap: putting pressure in kPa (61.64) gives 8.19 × 10⁻⁴, and using the universal constant 8.314 gives 28.3; 1.225 is only the sea-level value.

aero-w1-q4.question: An airliner cruises at 33,000 ft. Taking 1 ft = 0.3048 m, what is this altitude in km?
aero-w1-q4.explanation: 33,000 × 0.3048 = 10,058 m ≈ 10.06 km. Trap: dividing by 0.3048 instead of multiplying gives 108.3 km, which is above the atmosphere itself; always do a sanity check like this.

aero-w1-q5.question: A gas cell has a measured volume of 2.5 m³ and the air density is 1.225 kg/m³. How should the mass of air inside be written with correct significant digits?
aero-w1-q5.explanation: 1.225 × 2.5 = 3.0625, but 2.5 has only 2 significant digits, so the answer takes 2 s.f.: 3.1 kg. Trap: writing every calculator digit (3.0625) is false precision, and 3 kg keeps only 1 s.f.

aero-w1-q6.question: In the ISA troposphere, p/p₀ = (T/T₀)^5.256. At 11 km, T = 216.65 K, with T₀ = 288.15 K and p₀ = 101.325 kPa. What is the pressure at 11 km, approximately?
aero-w1-q6.explanation: T/T₀ = 216.65/288.15 = 0.752. (0.752)^5.256 ≈ 0.223, so p ≈ 0.223 × 101.325 ≈ 22.6 kPa. Trap: forgetting the exponent and using only the temperature ratio gives 76.2 kPa, and taking the exponent as 1/5.256 gives 96.0 kPa. Pressure falls much faster than temperature.

aero-w2-q1.question: A TV broadcast needs a satellite that always appears at the same spot from the ground, so home dishes never need to turn. Which orbit fits?
aero-w2-q1.explanation: A GEO satellite circles above the equator with the same period as Earth's rotation, so it looks fixed from the ground and a fixed dish works. Trap: 'sun-synchronous' also sounds synchronous, but it is synced with the Sun, not with Earth's surface; that satellite keeps moving across the sky.

aero-w2-q2.question: Which of these roles belongs to military aviation rather than civil aviation?
options: Refuelling fighters in the air (aerial refuelling tanker)
Spraying pesticide on farms with a drone
aero-w2-q2.explanation: Air-to-air refuelling of fighters is a military mission that extends the range of combat aircraft. Passenger flights, air ambulances and crop spraying are all civil applications. Trap: assuming any drone is military; drones are widely used for civil work too.

aero-w2-q3.question: A GEO satellite is directly above a ground station at 35,786 km. How long does a signal take to go from the ground to the satellite and back to the ground (one hop)? (c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
aero-w2-q3.explanation: Total distance = 2 × 35,786 km = 71,572 km = 7.157 × 10⁷ m. Time = 7.157 × 10⁷/(3 × 10⁸) ≈ 0.24 s. Trap: 0.12 s is only one leg (going up), and 0.48 s is two hops (question and reply), which is what you notice in a phone call.

aero-w2-q4.question: A survey drone has a 111 Wh battery, of which only 80% may be used. The drone draws 300 W. What flight time does it get?
aero-w2-q4.explanation: Usable energy = 0.8 × 111 = 88.8 Wh. Time = 88.8 / 300 = 0.296 h = 0.296 × 60 ≈ 17.8 min. Trap: forgetting the 80% gives 22.2 min, and not converting hours to minutes gives 0.30; 3.38 h comes from dividing power by energy.

aero-w2-q5.question: Why is a sun-synchronous orbit often chosen for remote-sensing (imaging) satellites?
options: The satellite passes over a place at the same local solar time each time, so lighting stays nearly the same across images
The satellite looks fixed at one spot from the ground
This orbit is the farthest from Earth, so the whole Earth is visible at once
In this orbit the satellite never gets sunlight
aero-w2-q5.explanation: The plane of a sun-synchronous orbit turns in step with the Sun, so the satellite passes at the same local time on each pass and shadows and lighting stay comparable, which matters for detecting changes. Trap: looking fixed from the ground is a GEO property, not a sun-synchronous one.

aero-w2-q6.question: An airliner burns 2,400 kg of fuel per hour in cruise and flies at 800 km/h with 180 passengers. How much fuel per passenger does a 1,200 km cruise take? (cruise only, ignore other phases)
aero-w2-q6.explanation: Time = 1,200/800 = 1.5 h. Total fuel = 2,400 × 1.5 = 3,600 kg. Per passenger = 3,600/180 = 20 kg. Trap: 3,600 kg is the fuel for the whole aircraft, 13.3 kg is the per-passenger fuel for one hour only (the 1.5 h was forgotten), and 0.0167 kg is per passenger per km.

aero-w3-q1.question: Which of these is an aerostat (lighter-than-air)?
aero-w3-q1.explanation: A hot-air balloon flies on the buoyancy of the hot, lighter air inside it, so it is an aerostat. The glider, helicopter and quadcopter are all heavier than air and fly on aerodynamic lift from a wing or rotor. Trap: a glider has no engine, but it still flies on wing lift.

aero-w3-q2.question: What is the main job of the tail rotor in a conventional helicopter?
options: Giving extra lift so more payload can be carried
Balancing the main rotor's reaction torque and giving yaw control
Blowing air to keep the engine cool
aero-w3-q2.explanation: When the engine turns the main rotor, the reaction torque tries to spin the helicopter body the other way. The tail rotor gives sideways thrust that balances this torque, and by changing that thrust the pilot controls yaw. Trap: forward thrust comes from tilting the main rotor forward, not from the tail rotor.

aero-w3-q3.question: A helium balloon has a volume of 600 m³. ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³ and ρ_He = 0.169 kg/m³. What total mass (envelope + payload) can it lift?
aero-w3-q3.explanation: Net lift per m³ = 1.225 − 0.169 = 1.056 kg. Total = 1.056 × 600 ≈ 634 kg. Trap: 735 kg comes from forgetting to subtract the helium's own weight; 6,216 is really the force in newtons (634 × 9.81), so writing it in kg is a unit error.

aero-w3-q4.question: At sea level ρ_air = 1.225 kg/m³ (288.15 K) and ρ_He = 0.169 kg/m³. A hot-air balloon heats its air to 373.15 K (same pressure). For the same net lift, roughly how many times the volume of the helium balloon does the hot-air balloon need?
aero-w3-q4.explanation: ρ_hot = 1.225 × 288.15/373.15 ≈ 0.946, so the hot-air lift is 1.225 − 0.946 = 0.279 kg/m³. Helium lift is 1.056 kg/m³. Ratio = 1.056/0.279 ≈ 3.78. Trap: 1.30 is just the ratio of temperatures (or densities), not of net lift; 0.26 comes from taking the ratio upside down.

aero-w3-q5.question: A quadcopter has a mass of 1.5 kg (g = 9.81 m/s²). In steady hover, how much thrust must each motor give?
aero-w3-q5.explanation: Weight = 1.5 × 9.81 = 14.7 N. In hover total thrust = weight, shared equally by four motors: 14.7/4 ≈ 3.68 N. Trap: 14.7 N is the thrust of the whole drone; 7.36 N is needed for a thrust-to-weight of 2 (maximum thrust for manoeuvring), not for hover.

aero-w3-q6.question: A 1,000 m³ helium balloon can lift 1,056 kg at sea level (ρ_air = 1.225, ρ_He = 0.169 kg/m³). At 3 km ρ_air = 0.909 and ρ_He = 0.126 kg/m³. If the volume stays the same, what mass can it lift at 3 km?
aero-w3-q6.explanation: Net lift at 3 km = (0.909 − 0.126) × 1,000 = 783 kg. Both air and helium get thinner, so lift falls roughly by the air-density ratio (0.909/1.225 ≈ 0.74). Trap: assuming the same volume gives the same lift (1,056 kg); 1,099 kg comes from mixing the sea-level air density with the 3 km helium density.

aero-w4-q1.question: Wing flutter is a vibration that grows when air forces combine with the wing's elasticity. Which two fields are mainly needed together to understand it?
aero-w4-q1.explanation: In flutter, aerodynamic forces bend the wing and the bending changes the forces; this is an interaction of aerodynamics and structures (elasticity), called aeroelasticity. Trap: linking every vibration to the engine and picking propulsion.

aero-w4-q2.question: Which of these tasks belongs to the ground support field?
options: Choosing an airfoil for the wing
Designing the cooling of turbine blades
aero-w4-q2.explanation: Ground support covers everything that helps operate the vehicle from the ground: maintenance, refuelling, air traffic control, airports, launch sites and mission control. Choosing an airfoil is aerodynamics, a control law is flight dynamics and control, and turbine cooling is propulsion.

aero-w4-q3.question: A light aircraft has a mass of 1,100 kg and a wing area of 16.2 m² (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is its wing loading?
aero-w4-q3.explanation: W = 1,100 × 9.81 = 10,791 N. W/S = 10,791/16.2 ≈ 666 N/m². Trap: 67.9 is really in kg/m² (g was forgotten) but is labelled N/m²; 1.50 × 10⁻³ is the inverse ratio S/W, and 174,800 comes from multiplying weight by area.

aero-w4-q4.question: A twin-engine airliner has 120 kN of thrust per engine and a take-off mass of 75,000 kg (g = 9.81 m/s²). What is its thrust-to-weight ratio at take-off?
aero-w4-q4.explanation: Total thrust = 2 × 120 = 240 kN. Weight = 75,000 × 9.81 = 735,750 N. T/W = 240,000/735,750 ≈ 0.33. Trap: using only one engine gives 0.16, forgetting g gives 3.2 (newtons divided by kg), and taking the ratio upside down gives 3.07.

aero-w4-q5.question: An aircraft has a fixed MTOW of 80,000 kg. Operating empty weight is 44,000 kg and mission fuel is 20,000 kg. New, more reliable avionics add 1,500 kg to the empty weight, with fuel unchanged. What is the maximum payload now?
aero-w4-q5.explanation: Before, payload = 80,000 − 44,000 − 20,000 = 16,000 kg. With an empty weight of 45,500 kg, payload = 80,000 − 45,500 − 20,000 = 14,500 kg. With MTOW fixed, every extra kg of structure or avionics comes straight out of payload. Trap: 17,500 kg comes from adding the 1,500 instead of subtracting it, and 36,000 kg from forgetting the fuel.

aero-w4-q6.question: Stall speed V_s = √(2W/(ρ S C_Lmax)). Keeping weight and C_Lmax the same, a designer increases wing area by 25%. How does the stall speed change?
aero-w4-q6.explanation: V_s ∝ 1/√S. New S = 1.25 S, so new V_s = V_s/√1.25 = 0.894 V_s, i.e. about 10.6% lower. Trap: forgetting the square root and using 1/1.25 = 0.8 (20% lower), or simply assuming 25% lower. The gain (lower stall speed) comes with the cost of a heavier wing and more drag.

aero-w5-q1.question: What is the 'chord' of an airfoil?
options: The mean curved line between the upper and lower surfaces
The straight line joining the leading edge and the trailing edge
The distance from one wingtip to the other
The maximum thickness of the airfoil
aero-w5-q1.explanation: The chord is the straight line from the leading edge to the trailing edge, and the angle of attack is measured from this line. Trap: the mean curved line is the camber line, and the wingtip-to-wingtip distance is the wingspan.

aero-w5-q2.question: If the airspeed is doubled while density, wing area and C_L stay the same, what happens to lift?
aero-w5-q2.explanation: In L = ½ρV²SC_L, lift is proportional to V². Doubling V ⇒ V² becomes four times ⇒ lift becomes 4 times. Trap: treating lift as proportional to V and saying 2 times.

aero-w5-q3.question: At sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) a wing flies at 50 m/s. Wing area is 16 m² and C_L = 0.6. What is the lift?
aero-w5-q3.explanation: q = ½ × 1.225 × 50² = 1,531.25 Pa. L = q S C_L = 1,531.25 × 16 × 0.6 = 14,700 N. Trap: forgetting the ½ gives 29,400 N, not squaring V gives 294 N, and forgetting C_L gives 24,500 N.

aero-w5-q4.question: An airliner flies at 11 km at 250 m/s (true airspeed), where the speed of sound is 295 m/s. What is its Mach number?
aero-w5-q4.explanation: M = V/a = 250/295 ≈ 0.847, i.e. high subsonic, at the edge of transonic. Trap: using the sea-level speed of sound of 340 m/s gives 0.735; 1.18 and 1.36 come from taking the ratio upside down.

aero-w5-q5.question: A wing has a chord of 1.2 m and flies at 40 m/s at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, μ = 1.8 × 10⁻⁵ Pa·s). What is the Reynolds number based on chord?
aero-w5-q5.explanation: Re = ρVc/μ = (1.225 × 40 × 1.2)/(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) = 58.8/(1.8 × 10⁻⁵) ≈ 3.27 × 10⁶. Trap: forgetting ρ gives 2.67 × 10⁶, and taking the ratio upside down (μ/ρVc) gives 3.06 × 10⁻⁷, which is dimensionless but is not Re.

aero-w5-q6.question: An aircraft has a mass of 1,000 kg, a wing area of 15 m² and C_Lmax = 1.5. What is its level-flight stall speed at sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, g = 9.81 m/s²)?
aero-w5-q6.explanation: W = 9,810 N. V_s = √(2W/(ρ S C_Lmax)) = √(19,620/(1.225 × 15 × 1.5)) = √(19,620/27.5625) = √711.8 ≈ 26.7 m/s. Trap: dropping the 2 in the formula gives 18.9 m/s, forgetting the square root gives 712, and forgetting g (treating mass as weight) gives 8.52 m/s.

aero-w6-q1.question: The pilot moves the control stick to the left. Which control surface acts, and about which axis does the aircraft rotate?
aero-w6-q1.explanation: Moving the stick left or right works the ailerons: one goes up and the other down, so one wing gains lift and the other loses it, and the aircraft rolls about the longitudinal axis. Trap: seeing the aircraft turn and thinking of yaw or the rudder; a turn starts with roll (bank).

aero-w6-q2.question: About which axis does pitch motion (nose up and down) take place?
aero-w6-q2.explanation: When the nose moves up and down, the wingtip-to-wingtip line stays in place, so pitch is about the lateral axis. Trap: hearing 'nose' and choosing the longitudinal axis; rotation about the longitudinal axis is roll.

aero-w6-q3.question: An aircraft's neutral point is at 0.42 c̄ of the mean chord and its CG is at 0.28 c̄ (both from the leading edge). What are the static margin and the stability?
aero-w6-q3.explanation: SM = (x_NP − x_CG)/c̄ = 0.42 − 0.28 = 0.14 = 14%. The CG is ahead of the neutral point, so the aircraft is statically stable. Trap: subtracting the wrong way round to get −14%, or using a ratio like 0.28/0.42 = 0.67, which is not the definition of static margin.

aero-w6-q4.question: In an aircraft the wing lift is 12,000 N and acts 0.15 m behind the CG. The horizontal tail is 5 m behind the CG. Ignore other moments. What force must the tail give for trim?
aero-w6-q4.explanation: The wing's nose-down moment = 12,000 × 0.15 = 1,800 N·m. To cancel it the tail must give a nose-up moment; the tail is behind the CG, so its force must act downward: F = 1,800/5 = 360 N downward. Trap: 1,800 is a moment (N·m), not a force; and an upward tail force would add to the nose-down moment.

aero-w6-q5.question: If an aircraft's vertical tail is made much smaller, which stability is most directly affected?
options: No stability changes, only drag falls
Lateral (roll) stability, which comes from dihedral
aero-w6-q5.explanation: The vertical tail works like a weathercock: in a sideslip it gets a side force that turns the nose back into the relative wind. So a smaller vertical tail reduces directional (yaw) stability. Trap: pitch stability comes from the horizontal tail and CG position, and roll stability mainly from dihedral.

aero-w6-q6.question: An aircraft has a mean chord c̄ = 2 m, its neutral point is at 0.40 c̄ and its CG starts at 0.25 c̄. During flight, fuel burn moves the CG 0.36 m aft. What are the static margin and stability now?
aero-w6-q6.explanation: CG shift = 0.36/2 = 0.18 c̄, so the new CG = 0.25 + 0.18 = 0.43 c̄. SM = 0.40 − 0.43 = −0.03 = −3%, so the CG is now behind the neutral point and the aircraft is statically unstable. Trap: adding the 0.36 m directly without dividing by the chord gives −21%, and ignoring the shift gives +15%.

aero-w7-q1.question: Which pressure does an aircraft's pressure altimeter use to show altitude?
aero-w7-q1.explanation: The altimeter takes the outside static pressure from the static port and converts it to altitude using the standard-atmosphere relation. Trap: total and dynamic pressure depend on speed, so they are used by the ASI; cabin pressure is inside the aircraft and does not tell the outside altitude.

aero-w7-q2.question: What do the gyroscopes in an IMU measure directly?
options: Angular rate (how fast it is rotating)
aero-w7-q2.explanation: Gyroscopes measure angular rate (rad/s or deg/s); integrating it gives attitude. Linear acceleration is measured by accelerometers, and magnetic heading comes from a magnetometer or compass. Trap: swapping the jobs of the accelerometer and the gyro.

aero-w7-q3.question: At sea level (ρ = 1.225 kg/m³) the difference between pitot and static pressure is 2,450 Pa. What is the airspeed?
aero-w7-q3.explanation: V = √(2Δp/ρ) = √(2 × 2,450/1.225) = √4,000 ≈ 63.2 m/s. Trap: forgetting the 2 gives √2,000 = 44.7 m/s, forgetting the square root gives 4,000, and using 4 instead of 2 gives 89.4 m/s.

aero-w7-q4.question: An aircraft's equivalent airspeed (EAS) is 80 m/s at an altitude where ρ = 0.736 kg/m³ (ρ₀ = 1.225 kg/m³). What is the true airspeed?
aero-w7-q4.explanation: TAS = EAS × √(ρ₀/ρ) = 80 × √(1.225/0.736) = 80 × 1.290 ≈ 103 m/s. In thinner air a higher true speed is needed for the same dynamic pressure. Trap: taking the ratio upside down gives 62.0 m/s, and forgetting the square root gives 133 m/s.

aero-w7-q5.question: During a climb the static port is completely blocked by ice (the pitot tube is fine). What will the altimeter show?
options: It keeps showing the correct altitude
It stays stuck at the altitude where the blockage happened
It shows a rise much faster than the real altitude
aero-w7-q5.explanation: The altimeter works only on static pressure. Once the port is blocked, the pressure inside stays at its value at the moment of blockage, so the altimeter sticks at that altitude and the VSI shows zero. Trap: thinking that no pressure means a zero reading; the trapped air keeps its pressure.

aero-w7-q6.question: Near sea level a drone's barometric sensor sees the static pressure drop from 101,325 Pa to 100,123 Pa. Taking ρ = 1.225 kg/m³ and g = 9.81 m/s² (Δp = ρgΔh), how far did the drone climb?
aero-w7-q6.explanation: Δp = 101,325 − 100,123 = 1,202 Pa. Δh = Δp/(ρg) = 1,202/(1.225 × 9.81) = 1,202/12.02 ≈ 100 m. Trap: forgetting g gives 981 m, multiplying by ρg gives about 14,400, and treating 1 Pa as 1 m gives 1,202 m.

aero-w8-q1.question: Which engine cannot give thrust to an aircraft standing on the runway (zero forward speed)?
aero-w8-q1.explanation: A ramjet has no compressor; it needs high forward speed of the vehicle to compress the air. At zero speed there is no compression and so no thrust. Trap: treating the rocket as air-breathing too; a rocket carries its own oxidiser and gives thrust even at zero speed.

aero-w8-q2.question: Why does a rocket engine work even in space (vacuum)?
options: There is no drag in space, so no thrust is needed
It carries its own oxidiser along with the fuel
It takes oxygen in through an intake
aero-w8-q2.explanation: Combustion needs both fuel and oxidiser. A rocket carries both, so it needs no outside air and makes thrust in vacuum by throwing gas backwards. Trap: no drag does not mean no thrust is needed; thrust is needed to change speed (Δv).

aero-w8-q3.question: A turbojet flies at 220 m/s. Air mass flow is 80 kg/s and exhaust velocity is 520 m/s. The nozzle is fully expanded and fuel mass is ignored. What is the net thrust?
aero-w8-q3.explanation: F = ṁ(V_e − V₀) = 80 × (520 − 220) = 80 × 300 = 24,000 N = 24.0 kN. Trap: forgetting the momentum of the incoming air and taking ṁV_e = 41.6 kN, or adding the velocities to get 59.2 kN.

aero-w8-q4.question: A total of 600 kg/s of air passes through a turbofan with a bypass ratio of 9. How much air goes through the core (the part with the combustor)?
aero-w8-q4.explanation: BPR = bypass/core = 9, so total = core + 9 × core = 10 × core. Core = 600/10 = 60 kg/s and bypass = 540 kg/s. Trap: dividing the total straight by 9 to get 66.7 kg/s, or taking the bypass flow (540) as the core.

aero-w8-q5.question: A rocket engine gives 750 kN of thrust in vacuum and burns 250 kg/s of propellant. Taking g₀ = 9.81 m/s², what is its specific impulse?
aero-w8-q5.explanation: I_sp = F/(ṁg₀) = 750,000/(250 × 9.81) = 750,000/2,452.5 ≈ 306 s. The effective exhaust velocity is 3,000 m/s. Trap: 3,000 is a velocity (m/s), not seconds; not converting kN to N gives 0.306, and multiplying by g₀ instead of dividing gives 29,430.

aero-w8-q6.question: A rocket stage has an initial mass of 50,000 kg and a burnout mass of 12,500 kg. The engine has I_sp = 300 s and g₀ = 9.81 m/s². What ideal Δv does the Tsiolkovsky equation give?
aero-w8-q6.explanation: Mass ratio = 50,000/12,500 = 4. Δv = I_sp g₀ ln 4 = 300 × 9.81 × 1.386 ≈ 4,080 m/s = 4.08 km/s. Trap: multiplying by the mass ratio instead of taking ln gives 11.77 km/s, using log₁₀ gives 1.77 km/s, and forgetting g₀ gives 0.416 km/s.

aero-w9-q1.question: What is the main job of ribs in a wing structure?
options: Carrying the main bending load along the span
Keeping the airfoil shape and passing skin loads to the spars
aero-w9-q1.explanation: Ribs are chord-wise frames that keep the airfoil shape, support the skin and stringers and transfer their loads to the spars. Trap: the main bending load is carried by the spar, not the rib; landing shocks are taken by the landing gear's shock absorber.

aero-w9-q2.question: In a semi-monocoque fuselage, what carries the load?
options: The skin together with frames and stringers
aero-w9-q2.explanation: In a semi-monocoque the thin skin does not carry load alone; frames and stringers support it and they all share the load. Trap: 'only the skin' is the definition of a pure monocoque.

aero-w9-q3.question: A 1,200 kg aircraft makes a level turn at 60° bank (g = 9.81 m/s²). How much lift must the wings produce?
aero-w9-q3.explanation: In a level turn n = 1/cos 60° = 2. W = 1,200 × 9.81 = 11,772 N, so L = nW = 23,544 N. Trap: taking n = 1 and writing just the weight (11,772 N); 13,593 N comes from using cos 30°, and 2,400 from forgetting g.

aero-w9-q4.question: A landing gear strut carries an axial load of 60 kN and has a cross-sectional area of 5 cm². What is the normal stress in the strut?
aero-w9-q4.explanation: A = 5 cm² = 5 × 10⁻⁴ m². σ = F/A = 60,000/(5 × 10⁻⁴) = 1.2 × 10⁸ Pa = 120 MPa. Trap: converting cm² with 10⁻³ or 10⁻⁵ gives 12 or 1,200 MPa, and not changing kN to N gives 0.12 MPa.

aero-w9-q5.question: An aircraft has a positive limit load factor of 3.8 and a factor of safety of 1.5. For what ultimate load factor must the structure be designed?
aero-w9-q5.explanation: Ultimate = limit × factor of safety = 3.8 × 1.5 = 5.7. Trap: dividing 3.8 by 1.5 gives 2.53, and adding them gives 5.3; the factor of safety multiplies.

aero-w9-q6.question: A pressurised fuselage has a radius of 1.9 m and a skin thickness of 1.6 mm. The pressure difference between cabin and outside is 55 kPa. What is the hoop stress in the skin (σ = Δp·r/t)?
aero-w9-q6.explanation: σ = 55,000 × 1.9/0.0016 = 6.53 × 10⁷ Pa ≈ 65.3 MPa. Trap: 32.7 MPa is the longitudinal stress (Δp·r/(2t)); leaving the thickness in mm gives 0.0653 MPa, and using the diameter instead of the radius gives 130.6 MPa.

aero-w10-q1.question: When a CFRP panel is joined directly with aluminium fasteners (in a humid environment), what is the biggest problem?
options: Galvanic corrosion: the aluminium corrodes quickly
No problem, both are light materials
aero-w10-q1.explanation: Carbon fibre and aluminium differ widely in electrochemical potential; in contact with moisture they form a galvanic cell and the aluminium (the anode) corrodes quickly. That is why titanium fasteners or insulation are used with CFRP. Trap: assuming that two light materials must also be compatible.

aero-w10-q2.question: In the context of materials, what is 'fatigue failure'?
options: Cracks growing under repeated (cyclic) loads, even at stresses below the static strength, until the part breaks
Breaking at once under a single very large load
The material melting at very high temperature
aero-w10-q2.explanation: In fatigue each load cycle grows the crack a little, and after thousands or millions of cycles the part can break even though the stress in each cycle is well below the static strength. Trap: breaking under a single overload is static failure, and rust is corrosion.

aero-w10-q3.question: Al alloy: σ = 500 MPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³. Ti alloy: σ = 900 MPa, ρ = 4,430 kg/m³. Based on specific strength (σ/ρ), which statement is correct?
options: Ti has higher strength, but Al's specific strength is about 2 times Ti's
aero-w10-q3.explanation: Al: 500 × 10⁶/2,800 ≈ 179 kN·m/kg. Ti: 900 × 10⁶/4,430 ≈ 203 kN·m/kg. Ti is slightly ahead, but against a 1.8 times gap in strength the specific strength differs by only about 14%, because Ti is also heavier. Trap: overestimating the effect of density and putting Al ahead.

aero-w10-q4.question: Steel (E = 200 GPa, ρ = 7,850 kg/m³), Al (E = 72 GPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³), Ti (E = 110 GPa, ρ = 4,430 kg/m³) and CFRP along the fibres (E = 135 GPa, ρ = 1,600 kg/m³). Which statement about specific stiffness (E/ρ) is correct?
options: Steel has the largest E, so its specific stiffness is also the highest
Al's specific stiffness is about 3 times that of steel
Ti's specific stiffness is higher than CFRP's
All three metals are at about 25 MN·m/kg, while CFRP is at about 84 MN·m/kg
aero-w10-q4.explanation: Steel 200/7.85 ≈ 25.5, Al 72/2.8 ≈ 25.7, Ti 110/4.43 ≈ 24.8 MN·m/kg, so the three metals are about equal. CFRP 135/1.6 ≈ 84.4 MN·m/kg. Trap: looking only at E and putting steel ahead; its density is just as much higher. Al's E is about 3 times lower than steel's, not its specific stiffness 3 times higher.

aero-w10-q5.question: A tension member is made of aluminium (σ_allow = 500 MPa, ρ = 2,800 kg/m³) and has a mass of 12 kg. If it is made of titanium (σ_allow = 900 MPa, ρ = 4,430 kg/m³) for the same load and length (area = load/σ_allow), what is the new mass?
aero-w10-q5.explanation: For the same load, area ∝ 1/σ, and mass = ρ × area × length, so mass ∝ ρ/σ. New mass = 12 × (4,430/900)/(2,800/500) = 12 × 4.922/5.6 ≈ 10.5 kg. Trap: using only the density ratio gives 19.0 kg, and only the strength ratio gives 6.67 kg; both apply together.

aero-w10-q6.question: A fitting has run 30,000 cycles at a stress level where its fatigue life is 150,000 cycles, and 8,000 cycles at a higher stress level where its life is 20,000 cycles. By Miner's rule (D = Σ n/N, failure at D = 1), how many more cycles can it run at the higher stress level?
aero-w10-q6.explanation: Damage so far = 30,000/150,000 + 8,000/20,000 = 0.2 + 0.4 = 0.6. Damage left = 1 − 0.6 = 0.4. Cycles at the higher stress = 0.4 × 20,000 = 8,000. Trap: treating the used damage 0.6 as what is left gives 12,000, ignoring the earlier cycles gives 20,000, and multiplying by the low-stress life (150,000) gives 60,000.

aero-w11-q1.question: Why does a GEO satellite appear fixed at one spot in the sky from the ground?
options: It circles above the equator, in the direction of Earth's rotation, with a period of one sidereal day
It stops in orbit because gravity is balanced there
It is in a polar orbit that turns with the Earth
It is so far away that gravity becomes zero there
aero-w11-q1.explanation: A GEO satellite's period equals Earth's rotation (23 h 56 min), and it moves in the equatorial plane in the same direction, so it keeps pace with the ground. It is moving at about 3.07 km/s, not standing still. Trap: assuming gravity is zero; there is gravity even at 42,164 km and it is what keeps the satellite in orbit.

aero-w11-q2.question: How does the orbital speed of a satellite in LEO compare with that of a GEO satellite?
options: Lower, because there is a little air drag in LEO
Equal, because all satellites have the same speed
Higher, because r is smaller in v = √(GM/r)
aero-w11-q2.explanation: v = √(GM/r): smaller r ⇒ higher v. About 7.7 km/s in LEO and about 3.1 km/s in GEO. Trap: thinking r is in the numerator and saying 'lower'; drag is not what sets the speed, it only slowly lowers the orbit.

aero-w11-q3.question: A satellite is in a circular orbit at 500 km altitude. Taking GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s² and R_earth = 6,371 km, what is its orbital speed?
aero-w11-q3.explanation: r = 6,371 + 500 = 6,871 km = 6.871 × 10⁶ m. v = √((3.986 × 10¹⁴)/(6.871 × 10⁶)) ≈ 7,617 m/s ≈ 7.62 km/s. Trap: using only the altitude (500 km) as r gives 28.2 km/s, using just R_earth gives 7.91 km/s, and not converting km to m gives 241 km/s.

aero-w11-q4.question: What is the orbital period of the same satellite (r = 6,871 km, v ≈ 7,617 m/s)?
aero-w11-q4.explanation: T = 2πr/v = 2π × 6.871 × 10⁶/7,617 ≈ 5,668 s ≈ 94.5 min. Trap: forgetting 2π and using r/v gives 15.0 min, using R_earth instead of r gives 87.6 min, and writing the seconds as minutes gives 5,669.

aero-w11-q5.question: A satellite's circular orbit radius (from Earth's centre) is made 4 times larger. By Kepler's third law, how many times longer is its period?
aero-w11-q5.explanation: T² ∝ r³ ⇒ T ∝ r^(3/2). r 4 times ⇒ T = 4^(3/2) = (√4)³ = 2³ = 8 times. Trap: treating T as proportional to r and saying 4 times, or reading T² ∝ r³ as T ∝ r² and saying 16 times.

aero-w11-q6.question: A spacecraft is in a circular orbit at 400 km altitude (r = 6,771 km, GM = 3.986 × 10¹⁴ m³/s²). What minimum extra Δv is needed to escape Earth's gravity from this point (one quick burn along the direction of motion)?
aero-w11-q6.explanation: v_circ = √((3.986 × 10¹⁴)/(6.771 × 10⁶)) ≈ 7.67 km/s. v_esc = √2 × 7.67 ≈ 10.85 km/s. Extra Δv = 10.85 − 7.67 ≈ 3.18 km/s, because the spacecraft is already moving at 7.67 km/s. Trap: taking the full escape speed (10.85) as the Δv, or using the escape speed from the surface (11.19 km/s).

aero-w12-q1.question: Which of these is a security issue rather than a safety issue?
options: A mistake by a tired pilot
Someone deliberately spoofing the GPS signal
A metal fatigue crack in the fuselage
aero-w12-q1.explanation: Security deals with deliberate harm; GPS spoofing is an intentional attack. A bird strike, a fatigue-related mistake and metal fatigue are all unintentional hazards, so they are safety issues. Trap: being confused because the word 'fatigue' appears in two options.

aero-w12-q2.question: What is the main aim of an aircraft accident investigation?
options: Finding the person responsible and getting them punished
Understanding the cause so that similar accidents do not happen again
Deciding the amount of the airline's insurance claim
aero-w12-q2.explanation: In international practice the purpose of a safety investigation is prevention: understanding what happened and why, and making safety recommendations. Blame and liability are separate processes. Trap: taking the focus on blame in the news as the aim of the investigation.

aero-w12-q3.question: An aircraft has three independent hydraulic systems. Each has a probability of 10⁻⁴ of failing in a flight hour. What is the probability that all three fail together?
aero-w12-q3.explanation: For independent events, P(all three fail) = 10⁻⁴ × 10⁻⁴ × 10⁻⁴ = 10⁻¹². Trap: adding the probabilities gives 3 × 10⁻⁴ (that is roughly the chance that at least one fails), and using only two systems gives 10⁻⁸.

aero-w12-q4.question: A navigation chain has 4 components in series (all must work). Each component has a reliability of 0.98. What is the reliability of the whole chain?
aero-w12-q4.explanation: Series system: R = 0.98⁴ = 0.98 × 0.98 × 0.98 × 0.98 ≈ 0.922. Every extra series component lowers reliability. Trap: 0.99999984 is the answer for a parallel system (1 − 0.02⁴), and 3.92 comes from adding reliabilities, which is impossible since it exceeds 1.

aero-w12-q5.question: Three identical flight computers run exactly the same software. Which kind of failure can this triple redundancy not protect against?
options: The power supply of one computer failing
A random hardware fault in one computer's chip
A software bug that triggers in all three on the same input (common-mode failure)
A loose connector on one computer
aero-w12-q5.explanation: A bug in identical software appears in all three computers at once on the same input, so voting finds all three wrong; this is a common-mode failure. A random fault in one computer is outvoted by the other two. That is why critical systems use dissimilar software and hardware. Trap: assuming three copies protect against every failure.

aero-w12-q6.question: A triplex sensor system uses 2-out-of-3 voting (at least two sensors must be correct). Each sensor has a reliability of 0.95 and the sensors are independent. What is the system reliability?
aero-w12-q6.explanation: R = 3r² − 2r³ = 3 × 0.9025 − 2 × 0.857375 = 2.7075 − 1.71475 ≈ 0.993. Trap: 0.857 = 0.95³ (all three must be correct), and 0.999875 = 1 − 0.05³ (any one is enough), which is not the condition for a voting system.
